title: Boundaries after
hookLine: forgiveness and safety can go together

cards: A woman forgives her brother for borrowing money and never paying it back. She means it; the bitterness is gone. A month later he calls, warm and friendly, and asks to borrow again.
Here's the question that can trip people up: if she's really forgiven him, doesn't she have to say yes? Doesn't saying no mean she's still holding it against him?
Genesis has a story about a man who tested the lock before he opened the door to his brothers. Today: boundaries after.

teach.b: First, Joseph. His brothers sold him into slavery. Years later he's governor in Egypt, and in a famine the same brothers arrive to buy grain.
They don't recognize him. He recognizes them, and he doesn't rush to embrace them. He tests them.
He keeps one brother as a hostage, then frames the youngest, Benjamin, and watches what the others will do. Will they abandon this brother the way they abandoned him? Second, the answer.
Judah, the brother who once suggested selling Joseph, offers to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place.
Only then does Joseph break down: "I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt." He weeps and kisses his brothers, after he has watched what they do.
One way to read the testing: he waited to see whether they had changed before he let them close. Third, the wisdom books are practical about safety.

teach.h: WITH A FURIOUS MAN THOU SHALT NOT GO.
teach.b: Proverbs says: "Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go: Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul." That isn't hatred. It's caution.
Some people aren't safe to walk beside, and the texts don't ask anyone to pretend otherwise. Fourth, how the two fit. Forgiveness lives inside you: you let go of the debt, the bitterness, the replay.

teach.h: INSIDE, AND IN WHAT YOU DO.
teach.b: A boundary lives in what you do: what you lend, where you go, when you answer the phone.
The sister can forgive her brother completely and still say: I'm not lending money again. That's not a grudge. It's a door with a lock.

how: Some counselors, pastors and rabbis teach that forgiveness does not require trusting someone again right away, and point to Joseph's testing of his brothers in Genesis 42–45 as a story of forgiveness that waited to see change.

o: walls you put up to punish someone until they've apologized
rules for the other person that they must agree to follow
letting go inside, while still protecting yourself in what you do

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: offered to stay in Benjamin's place
with a furious man thou shalt not go

s: Joseph revealed himself to his brothers the moment they arrived
he tested them first, and revealed himself after Judah offered to take Benjamin's place.
the brother who offered to stay in Benjamin's place was Judah, who once suggested selling Joseph
in Genesis 44 Judah offers himself as a slave instead of Benjamin; Joseph reveals himself right after.
Proverbs advises against friendship with an angry man
"Make no friendship with an angry man."

games.q: you've truly forgiven your brother for a loan he never paid back. now he calls, friendly, and asks to borrow again. what fits today's teaching?
o: lend it, or the forgiveness wasn't real.
keep the forgiveness, and still say no to the loan.
refuse, and remind him what he did last time.
games.why: forgiveness lives inside you; a boundary lives in what you do. one doesn't cancel the other. that's not a grudge, it's a door with a lock.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've forgiven, or are trying to, where something still needs protecting: your time, your money, your peace, your body.
Name the boundary in one plain sentence, like I leave when the shouting starts, or I don't answer after ten at night, and say it silently, without anger.
Notice that you can wish them well and still keep it, and if you pray, pray for them and for your own safety in the same breath.

wordCard.voice: Boundaries after. Letting go of the bitterness inside, while still protecting what needs protecting in what you do. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: forgive and stay safe. Letting go and locking the door can both be kind. Day nine hundred eighty-six, done.
